Is Waz a Business and an Art Form, or a Noble Mission of Propagating the Din? — When Commercial Mindsets, Self-Promotion, and the Competition for Entertainment Take Over the Platform of Da‘wah!

Regrettably, a section of the ‘Ulama and Wā‘izīn in our society have gradually transformed Waz from a noble mission of propagating the Din into a commercial profession. For them, Waz is increasingly no longer an *Amanah* of ‘Ilm or a Prophetic responsibility; rather, it has become a means of earning money, a strategy for gaining popularity, and an instrument for expanding personal, group-based, and partisan influence.

For them, Waz has become more of an art form than an act of Da‘wah; more of a rhetorical performance than an act of sincere admonition; and more of an entertainment programme for audiences than a call towards self-purification.

In business, there is competition, advertising, flashy promotional campaigns, middlemen and brokers, bargaining, attempts to capture the market, jealousy and hostility towards competitors, and exaggeration or deception regarding the quality of products. Regrettably, these very tendencies are becoming increasingly visible in the world of Waz as well.

Just as attracting customers is the primary objective in business, attracting audiences seems to have become the overriding concern for many in the arena of Waz. How many thousands attended? How many slogans were chanted? How many rounds of applause were received? How many times did the audience become emotionally overwhelmed? How many views were generated? How many followers were gained? How much money was earned? These statistics increasingly appear to have become the principal measures of success in Waz.

Yet, how much ‘Ilm was actually imparted? How many misconceptions were corrected? How many people's thoughts and perspectives underwent positive transformation? How many improved their Iman, ‘Amal, and character? How many developed greater Taqwa and a sense of accountability in the Hereafter? These questions seem to be entirely absent from the calculation of success.

An increase in audience numbers does not necessarily mean greater success in Da‘wah. The volume of slogans cannot measure the depth of ‘Ilm, nor can the number of views determine the degree of Ikhlas.

Just as businesses use attractive packaging to make their products more appealing, many Waz programmes now place greater emphasis on vocal theatrics, gestures, emotional dramatization, humour, poetry, songs, and techniques for stirring up audiences than on the intellectual depth of their content. Deficiencies in ‘Ilm are compensated for through vocal artistry; weaknesses in textual evidence are concealed beneath an abundance of stories; and the hollowness of a speech is masked by excessive emotionalism.

Just as a business can be launched with very little capital, many people today enter the arena of Waz without any substantial scholarly capital. Some possess only a little, while others seem to have invested more in publicity than in knowledge itself. Many cannot even recite the Qur’an with proper Qira’ah, nor do they possess the ability to read the Arabic texts of Hadith accurately. Yet they confidently deliver incorrect translations and fabricated interpretations of the Qur’an and Hadith.

Their entire scholarly repertoire consists of an appealing voice, a few poems and songs, imitation of others, some memorized catchy phrases, emotionally charged presentations, and baseless anecdotes and fabricated stories. In some cases, the more glaring the deficiency in ‘Ilm, the greater the outward glamour of the presentation!

Yet speaking about the Din is neither an ordinary public speech nor merely an exercise in vocal performance. It requires extensive study, sound knowledge of the Qur’an and Sunnah, proficiency in the Arabic language, Fiqhi insight, historical awareness, and a profound understanding of the responsibility attached to every word one utters.

One may certainly move an audience emotionally through inaccurate recitation, erroneous translations, or fabricated interpretations of the Qur’an and Hadith. But that does not constitute service to the Din. Rather, it creates the danger of propagating ignorance in the name of Islam.

It must be remembered that a beautiful voice may enhance the appeal of a speech, and it may even be possible to make an audience laugh or cry. But none of these is a substitute for ‘Ilm. Vocal melodiousness is not intellectual depth, and an audience's admiration is not a certificate of religious scholarship.

Just as businesses have seasonal markets, a seasonal market for Waz has also emerged. As the particular season approaches, preachers become increasingly busy with bookings for religious gatherings, fee negotiations, promotional campaigns, and competition to outdo one another. In some instances, a speaker's popularity, online views, number of followers, and market rate receive greater consideration than his scholarly qualifications or the quality of his discourse.

Even more astonishing is that those who claim to be propagators of the Din sometimes engage in competition as though they were rival businessmen operating in the same marketplace! Who will surpass whom? Whose gathering will attract the largest audience? Who will receive the highest remuneration? Whose publicity will be more extensive? Who will have more followers? Such unhealthy competition often gives rise to mutual verbal abuse, hostility, and expressions of resentment. Some even resort to slander, misinformation, ridicule, and personal attacks in an attempt to undermine the credibility of others.

Such market-driven rivalry among those who propagate the Din is truly painful. The very platform from which lessons of brotherhood, tolerance, noble character, and mutual respect should be imparted becomes associated with individuals who compete to belittle one another. When this happens, the very moral foundation of their Da‘wah comes into question.

The question, therefore, is: Are these individuals serving the Din, or are they building their own personal market by exploiting the name of the Din?

Of course, accepting an honorarium or remuneration for delivering Waz is not, in itself, the issue. The need to earn a livelihood is a practical reality, just as the permissibility of receiving remuneration for certain forms of religious service is a recognized subject of Shar‘i discussion. The real concern arises when money becomes the ultimate objective, popularity becomes the measure of competence, self-promotion replaces Da‘wah, and the dignity of the Din becomes secondary to personal interests.

Receiving remuneration and turning the Din into a commodity are not the same thing. This distinction must be clearly understood. Accepting payment to meet one's livelihood needs is one reality; exploiting the Din for money, fame, and the expansion of personal influence is an entirely different matter.

The Da‘wah of Allah's Din is not a project for establishing an individual's personal brand. The Minbar of Waz is not an artist's stage where applause and audience admiration constitute the ultimate measure of success. It is an *Amanah* entrusted to us through the legacy of the Prophets and Messengers. Here, sincerity of intention should matter more than eloquence, ‘Ilm more than vocal performance, Ikhlas more than popularity, and the pleasure of Allah more than outward measures of success.

Earlier generations of Muslim scholars issued stern warnings against turning ‘Ilm and religious admonition into instruments for pursuing worldly interests.

Ibn ‘Abidin (Rahimahullah), in *Al-Durr al-Mukhtar*, mentions the following statement:

"Turning religious preaching and admonition into a means of accumulating wealth, attaining leadership, gaining public acceptance, or making people one's devoted followers is a form of misguidance and a practice characteristic of the Jews and Christians."

(*Al-Durr al-Mukhtar*, 6/421)

Imam al-Tabari (Rahimahullah), in *Tahdhib al-Athar*, reports:

*Man talaba al-‘ilma yubahi bihi al-‘ulama’a, aw liyumariya bihi al-sufaha’a, aw liyasrifa wujuh al-nasi ilayhi, fal-naru awla bihi.*

"Whoever seeks knowledge in order to boast before the scholars, argue with the ignorant, or turn people's attention towards himself and make them his followers, the Fire is more befitting for him."

(*Tahdhib al-Athar*)

A stern warning is also quoted in *Rabi‘ al-Abrar*:

*Waylun li-ummati min ‘ulama’i al-su’; yattakhidhuna al-‘ilma tijaratan yab‘i‘unaha, la arbahallahu tijaratahum.*

"Woe to the evil scholars of my Ummah, who turn knowledge into a commercial enterprise and buy and sell it for worldly gain. May Allah grant no profit to their trade!"

(*Rabi‘ al-Abrar*)

In essence, standing on the Minbar of Waz does not automatically make someone a servant of the Din. A beautiful voice, an emotionally charged presentation, a massive audience, or hundreds of thousands of social media followers can never substitute for ‘Ilm, Ikhlas, and Taqwa.

It must be remembered that the purpose of Da‘wah is not to make people devoted followers of the preacher, but to make them devoted servants of Allah. It is not to draw people towards oneself, but to guide them back to Allah. It is not to expand one's own recognition and influence, but to reform people's Iman, ‘Amal, and character.

If the very Minbar from which people's hearts should be awakened to the realities of the Hereafter becomes a centre for a preacher's worldly interests, personal publicity, and commercial competition, it not only undermines the very purpose of Da‘wah but also places the dignity of the Din in question.

**More alarming than turning the propagation of the Din into a profession is disguising professional self-interest behind the façade of propagating the Din.**
